claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 forms an amorphous structure under very rapid melt-spinning but forms multiple crystalline phases at slower cooling rates.
The baseline alloy has limited amorphous retention and complex crystallization behavior during reheating.
Phosphorus and high mixing entropy promote amorphous-phase formation in the baseline alloy during extremely rapid cooling.
Adding approximately 1–2 at.% Nb will improve glass-forming ability and amorphous-phase thermal stability.
Nb is a high-melting, sluggish-diffusing element in the proposed alloy.
The Nb intervention should be most effective during melt-spinning at approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s or accelerated cooling at approximately 3000 K/s.
At a cooling rate of approximately 52 K/s, 1–2 at.% Nb may be insufficient to prevent crystallization.
Nb increases atomic-size mismatch and introduces sluggish-diffusion kinetic barriers that suppress crystalline nucleation and growth.
Nb promotes a more uniform amorphous structure by interfering with phosphorus-rich or intermetallic-phase formation.
Nb lowers the driving force for crystallization by enhancing the free-energy difference between the amorphous state and competing crystalline phases.
Nb enlarges the supercooled-liquid region and raises the crystallization temperature during reheating.
Nb slows atomic rearrangement during thermal analysis.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the Nb-modified alloy will retain a robust amorphous structure over a wider range of rapid cooling conditions.
The Nb-modified alloy will show a higher crystallization-onset temperature and smaller DSC exothermic peaks during reheating.
Excessive Nb could cause segregation or unwanted Nb-rich secondary phases.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says that enhancing the free-energy difference between the amorphous and crystalline states lowers the crystallization driving force. Without specifying the sign or which state is stabilized, a larger free-energy difference would ordinarily imply a larger rather than smaller driving force, so the thermodynamic statement is internally incoherent.
